study.title: Exodus 35 The restored worship: Sabbath, offering and service enabled by God
study.overview: Exodus 35 Moses gathered the whole congregation to transmit, in a public and orderly manner, the divine instructions concerning the sabbath and the construction of the tabernacle. The chapter highlights three movements linked to each other: the holiness of rest on the seventh day, the voluntary participation of the people in the offerings for the work, and the choice of workers empowered by God to accurately execute what He commanded. The repetition of instructions given before is not mere literary detail; it reinforces that the sanctuary must be done exactly according to the word of the LORD, in contrast to the previous attempt to worship God in the very way, as in the case of the golden calf.

outline.title: The Sabbath as a Holy Commandment
outline.explanation: Moses summons the community and begins with what is urgent: the seventh day belongs to the LORD and must be kept as holy rest. The text emphasizes the seriousness of obedience, including the prohibition of lighting fire in the dwellings on that day, showing that rest is not an optional detail, but a central part of the covenant.

outline.title: The offers and the list of the work of the tabernacle
outline.explanation: Then Moses summons voluntary offerings of various materials, coming from all the people. The detailed list shows that each element of the tabernacle, from its furniture to the priestly garments, would depend on the generosity of the people and the plan given by God. The chapter underlines that true worship does not improvise: it follows an order received from the Lord.

outline.title: The voluntary and community response of the people
outline.explanation: The people withdraw and return bringing offerings with readiness. Men and women contribute metals, fabrics, leather, wood, olive oil and spices; wise women stood; the princes brought stones and aromas. The text insists on the voluntary heart, showing that participation in the cult was marked by inner disposition, not by coercion.

outline.title: Bezalel and Aoliab: God-givered ability
outline.explanation: Finally, Moses announces that God called Bezalel and filled him with the Spirit of God, granting wisdom, intelligence, and knowledge to every kind of artistic work. Aoliabe is also included as someone who teaches and assists. The work of the sanctuary thus appears as a technical and artistic service, but originated and empowered by God Himself.

study.context: The chapter is part of the section in which, after the restoration of the relationship between God and Israel, the construction of the tabernacle is resumed. The notes note that this part largely repeats instructions already given before, now with the change from the imperative to the description of compliance. This points out that the people have ceased to try to secure God's presence on their own and began to obey the ordained manner of Him. The notes also indicate that the congregation is convened through its representatives, and that the people respond immediately to the instructions received.
study.theology: The chapter presents a theology of reverent obedience. The Sabbath shows that the life of the people is governed not only by production and task, but by the holiness of the time belonging to the Lord. Voluntary offers show that worship requires generous participation, not just external obligation. The tabernacle, in turn, is not the fruit of autonomous religious creativity; it must be built according to the divine commandment. In addition, Bezalel and Aoliabe's empowerment teaches that practical and artistic skills also come from God and should be employed for his glory. Thus, the chapter unites rest, service and art under the authority of the Lord, without separating spirituality from work, nor religious zeal of order.

scholarViews.insight: The detailed repetition of the instruction on the tabernacle emphasizes that the work was done exactly as God had commanded, in contrast to the previous attempt to seek divine presence by its own means.

The convocation of the whole congregation shows that the representatives of the people receive the instructions of Moses to then communicate them to the community, preserving order in teaching and obedience.

Regarding the prohibition of burning fire on the Sabbath, the note notes that this order is understood by the Jews as a restriction on fire used for work or preparation of food, not necessarily for light and heat.

questions: What does the chapter teach about the difference between serving God according to his word and trying to do this in our own way?
How does the voluntary heart of the people contrast with a religion made only by obligation?
How does the empowerment given by God to Bezalel and Aoliabe correct the idea that only strictly "religious" tasks are spiritual?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine three areas: rest, generosity and service. First, we must honor the limits and holiness of God's time, without transforming the work into an absolute master of life. Second, the contribution to the work of God must be born from a willing heart, with readiness and joy, not of pressure. Third, every skill received is technical, artistic, manual or intellectual - should be seen as a gift of God to be used faithfully. In practice, this implies planning the rest before the Lord, offering resources and time with freedom of heart, and developing gifts to serve the church and others with excellence and humility.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are brief and do not cover every detail of the chapter with the same level of development. Therefore, the application and context were limited to what the text itself and the comments effectively support. There is no basis here to safely state additional details about geography, dates, specific customs beyond what was explicitly mentioned in the notes.
